transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-20
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Meyer (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Liam O'Connor (EmberCloud CTO); Maya Patel (Platform Eng); Diego Ruiz (Security); Ana Flores (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- EmberCloud evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + Dedicated capacity for latency-sensitive customer-facing features; exploring SDKs and gateway/proxy approach to centralize calls; interested in LangChain / LlamaIndex adapters and how rate limits/quotas would be enforced; security and observability hooks important.

Topics flagged: SDK onboarding, LangChain/LlamaIndex integration, gateway vs sidecar proxy, rate limiting strategies, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, observability hooks and tracing, KMS + audit logs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we'll do a short intro then dive into the integration questions. i'm jordan from redwood, ae on the account. priya is our se.
[00:18] Priya: hi all, quick wave, i'm priya, i'll try to cover the nitty gritty on the sdk and network options and some sample code.
[00:28] Liam: good to be here, thanks. we got a condensed agenda from ana earlier — main ask is: how do we plug redwood into our existing gateway architecture without reworking every service.
[00:42] Ana: yes also we need to understand quotas and how rate caps will behave during peak, and observability — we want traces into our datadog.
[00:54] Jordan: great, that's exactly what priya and i planned. quick context from our side — embercloud is building conversational assistants across multiple products, low-latency routing for logged-in users and compliance for certain enterprise customers. is that right, liam?
[01:08] Liam: exactly. we have a mix of latency-sensitive flows (sub-500ms token latency) and batch embeddings jobs overnight. some features need guaranteed isolation for data residency.
[01:20] Diego: and on the security side we need to see KMS integration, audit logs, sso/roles, and understand whether requests ever hit third-party memcache or anything that would store PII.
[01:34] Priya: quick clarifier — when you say gateway architecture, are you thinking of a centralized api gateway that routes to redwood, or a service-sidecar pattern where each service calls redwood directly through an internal proxy?
[01:48] Maya: we currently use an api gateway plus a small sidecar in some services. ideally we'd like a single point to enforce rate limits, but also not add too much latency for token generation paths.
[02:00] Jordan: ok, so two possible patterns: 1) gateway-forwarding: api gateway sends traffic to a dedicated redwood-proxy layer that we manage/host or you host as a sidecar; 2) sdk-first: services integrate redwood SDK directly and use our built-in batching and kv cache with a lightweight shim. priya will run through pros/cons.
[02:16] Priya: yeah, quick table in words — gateway-forwarding centralizes auth & quotas, easier observability; sidecar reduces cross-hop latency and lets you localize KV cache for prefixes. SDK direct is simplest for dev experience and gets you automatic batching, but you need to manage secrets per service or use short-lived tokens.
[02:36] Liam: for the latency numbers — when you say batching, is that automatic on the sdk? our concern is some web paths are sync calls.
[02:48] Priya: yes batching is workload-aware; by default SDK does small-window continuous batching and you can pin models to non-batched paths for strict latency. you can also set a max batching window — so synchronous flows can disable batching or set tiny windows. note small windows hurt throughput, obviously.
[03:06] Maya: can you talk a bit about langchain / llamain... llama index adapters — we have many of our retrieval layers written on langchain.
[03:18] Priya: absolutely — we provide an official langchain integration and a community LlamaIndex connector. the langchain adapter supports streaming responses and function/tool calling; the Llama Index connector currently hooks into the retriever interface — small caveat, some of the object names may be different in the index, we've seen transcript mislabels like "Llama Index" vs "LlamaIndex" in older docs. we'll send a sample repo.
[03:40] Jordan: (laughs) we also have an examples repo with a serverless demo using langchain + redis as the vector store. we'll share that.
[03:48] Diego: about rate limits — how are quotas enforced? per api key, per org, per route? and do you have burst allowances?
[03:58] Priya: we have hierarchical quotas — token and request quotas at the API key level and org level, plus route-level overrides. burst behavior can be configured — we allow a token-burst pool for short-term spikes if you have a Dedicated contract or reserved burst capacity. on Hosted, bursts are smaller; Dedicated gets configurable burst windows and higher SLAs.
[04:24] Liam: ok can we throttle per customer tenant within our org? like per-customer-id quotas?
[04:32] Priya: yes you can implement tenant-level quotas in two ways: 1) enforce at your gateway by mapping incoming customer-id to a specific API key with per-key quotas, or 2) use our per-route tagging and quota policies so you can apply limits to a route that includes customer-id. route tagging is helpful if you don't want to manage many API keys.
[04:54] Ana: curious about observability: does redwood emit traces and spans we can ingest? we use datadog and honeycomb in some teams.
[05:04] Priya: we emit prometheus-compatible metrics and have tracing headers that propagate; there is an opentelemetry collector integration you can point at, and we can send a compatibility guide for datadog. spans include model selection, queuing time, kernel time, and token time breakdown but sometimes the names are slightly different depending on model backend.
[05:26] Diego: are logs PII filtered? what does the audit log look like?
[05:32] Jordan: for Hosted we have configurable redaction, and audit logs that include request ids, API key, timestamp, route, and model version. we don't store full prompts in audit logs by default — you can opt-in to store masked prompts for debugging, or we can provide token-level hashes. for Dedicated/Private you control retention and can route logs to your Kinesis/S3.
[05:56] Liam: on Private: what exactly does private mean — a bookable on-prem box or VPC?
[06:04] Priya: Private = customer-controlled VPC deployment, optionally air-gapped on-prem package. the control plane can be hosted but API plane lives in your network. Dedicated is redwood-hosted reserved capacity, isolated tenancy; Hosted is multi-tenant. Benefits of Private include compliance and network isolation, but onboarding is longer and ops heavier.
[06:26] Maya: for Private, is there a sidecar or do we run an internal gateway?
[06:32] Priya: usually teams run an internal gateway that fronts the on-prem control plane, with sidecars for caching. we ship a helm chart for the proxy if you want to run a maintained version internally.
[06:44] [Speaker 1]: um can i jump in — is the helm chart maintained upstream or is it a one-off?
[06:50] Priya: it's maintained upstream by our infra team; you can pin chart versions. we support upgrade paths and we provide an operator for lifecycle hooks.
[06:58] Liam: the question about redis/kv — we have an existing redis cluster; can we use that for the prefix cache?
[07:06] Priya: you can either use our managed kv cache or point to your redis as the backing store; the SDK supports a pluggable cache adapter. caveat: TTL behavior and eviction patterns should be tuned — we'll share recommended settings.
[07:20] Ana: let's talk failure modes — if our gateway hits rate limit, do calls fail-fast? is there backpressure? we'd prefer graceful degradation.
[07:30] Jordan: good call; Redwood offers several fallback policies: soft-fail with cached response, fallback to a smaller model variant, or queue with retry/backoff. For Hosted we can configure automatic fallback to a cost-tier model on a per-route policy. In Dedicated, you can set local fallbacks and amplified burst pool.
[07:52] Priya: also note timeouts — we recommend client-side timeouts slightly higher than the model SLO so we get proper tracing and don't leak resources.
[07:58] Diego: security again — how do you handle KMS? we run keys in AWS KMS and HSM for some customers.
[08:06] Priya: we integrate with AWS KMS and also support customer-managed keys via HSM for Private. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption and per-tenant keying on enterprise plans. we'll include the KMS integration doc in the follow-up.
[08:20] Liam: what about per-call redaction or dynamic masking? we have PHI in some flows.
[08:26] Jordan: we have request-time redaction rules you can apply at the gateway layer and a prompt-scrubber plugin for the SDK. For higher compliance you should use Private and keep raw context out of the hosted audit logs.
[08:40] Ana: curious about developer experience — how long would it take for a service to ship with the sdk vs gateway approach?
[08:46] Priya: SDK integration for basic generation is typically a 1–2 day effort per service including auth, tests, and monitoring hooks. Gateway integration is 3–5 days to wire routes, quota mapping and observability because you centralize things but you save per-service work. sidecar approach usually sits between those numbers.
[09:06] Liam: would you recommend starting with hosted for evaluation and then moving to Dedicated if we need predictable throughput?
[09:12] Jordan: that's the normal pattern — POC on Hosted to validate quality and prompts, then move to Dedicated for capacity and SLAs; Private reserved for customers with strict compliance.
[09:22] Maya: can you share any specifics about latency for a medium-size model — say 8k context-ish? we run some 3–4k typical.
[09:30] Priya: model and hardware matter. from our benchmarks, an 8k context medium model on A100 equivalent in Dedicated median token time is ~30–40ms per token with optimizations; Hosted numbers are similar but subject to noisy neighbor variance. for 3–4k context you should see lower times. we'll share a benchmark sheet but caveat it depends on prompt length and kernel selection.
[09:56] Diego: do you support quantized variants and will the response quality be impacted?
[10:02] Priya: yes we support int8 and select int4 profiles. quantization guidance is model-specific and we have a small eval harness to compare quality/regression. Optimize tool gives suggestions on quantization vs latency tradeoffs.
[10:16] Jordan: quick check — are you planning a strict timeline for pilot?
[10:20] Ana: target pilot in Q3, ideally starting late august. decision for Dedicated by mid-september if pilot goes well.
[10:30] Jordan: perfect, that's actionable.
[10:34] [00:10:34] Priya: demo time — i'll pull up a quick architecture sketch. (brief pause, some typing noises)
[10:50] Priya: ok imagine path A: external request hits embercloud gateway -> gateway forwards to redwood-proxy -> proxy enforces auth, quota, tags route, calls Redwood API -> Redwood does batching, cache, responds. Path B: service calls redwood sdk directly, sdk handles token refresh via sts and does batching locally, cache optionally backed by local redis.
[11:12] Maya: for path A is the proxy a managed container or something we run?
[11:16] Priya: you can run our proxy as a managed service we host in your VPC (for Dedicated/Private) or you can deploy the helm chart in your cluster. For Hosted demo, we typically run a minimal shim in your gateway.
[11:26] Liam: how does authentication work — short lived credentials?
[11:30] Priya: yes for best practice: client obtains a short-lived JWT from your identity service, gateway exchanges for a short-lived API token with Redwood via the token exchange flow. SDK supports token refresh via sts.
[11:40] Diego: any limitations on session affinity? some of our flows depend on sticky sessions for prefix caching.
[11:46] Priya: our runtime has sticky prefix affinity policy — if you send a conversation id in headers we route to the same cache partition for lower KV misses. We recommend passing a conversation id header.
[11:58] Jordan: (interject) small note on quotas: if you want per-tenant strict limits, using API key mapping at gateway is simplest.
[12:06] Ana: what about observability metadata — can we tag spans with our internal customer_id and product phases?
[12:12] Priya: yes header propagation includes custom tags and we store them in trace metadata. you can also push logs to your s3 or pubsub for long-term retention.
[12:22] [00:12:22] Liam: there's a question about SDK languages — we primarily use go and node, a small python team.
[12:28] Priya: official SDKs in node and python today; go is community maintained but we have beta go SDK available. if go is important we'll prioritize support for a production-grade go client.
[12:38] Maya: will SDK support native otel instrumentation?
[12:42] Priya: yes, we have otel hooks in python/node, and the go beta includes basic otel. full coverage is on the roadmap.
[12:50] Diego: side question — do you do model monitoring for hallucination/regression? we need to detect drift.
[12:58] Priya: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to evals and prompt sets. You can set regression alerts when a metric crosses a threshold. We also support streaming outputs to your eval pipeline where you can run custom checks.
[13:12] Jordan: (quick) we'll follow up with the sample repo and the benchmark sheet.
[13:18] Ana: please also include a simple flow for VPC peering and egress IPs — our security team will need that.
[13:24] Diego: plus SOC2 and data retention docs.
[13:28] Jordan: noted.
[13:32] [00:13:32] Priya: back to rate limits — one thing to watch for: if you centralize through gateway and then suddenly a single route spikes you could run into a per-key cap. route-level throttles help. We also support leaky-bucket and token-bucket algorithms depending on the policy. For user-level fairness we recommend combining per-route tagging with a per-tenant token bucket.
[13:56] Liam: that's good to know. do you have throttling SDK primitives? like a client-side token bucket to shape traffic?
[14:02] Priya: there's a client-side rate limiter module in the SDK that you can enable. It honors server-provided X-RateLimit headers for dynamic shaping.
[14:12] Ana: about pricing — is bursting charged differently? how will we see cost per token per route?
[14:18] Jordan: bursts are metered separately when they come from the burst pool. in Dedicated we show token-per-route breakdowns and you get cost visibility in the console with route-level tags. Priya will show a screenshot in the follow-up.
[14:30] Maya: let's talk about a small POC architecture — we're thinking of building an internal gateway route that accepts customer chat then calls redwood. should we prototype with Hosted?
[14:38] Priya: yes start with Hosted to validate prompt quality and latency; for the POC we can provide a sandbox api key and a small credit bundle. If you need predictable latency for demo customers, consider a Dedicated pilot.
[14:52] Liam: what about data residency — one of our enterprise customers requires EU-only data. can Hosted commit to region constraints?
[15:00] Jordan: Hosted can serve regionally but for firm residency controls we recommend Dedicated or Private with explicit region placement. Hosted has region options but not hard contractual residency guarantees unless part of enterprise agreement.
[15:14] Diego: any notes on encryption in transit and at rest?
[15:18] Priya: TLS everywhere in transit, at-rest encryption with customer-managed KMS on enterprise plans, and HSM options for Private.
[15:28] [00:15:28] Ana: one practical ask — can you provide a simple langchain example that uses our vector store? we use elastic plus a managed pinecone like service internally.
[15:38] Priya: sure — we have a langchain connector example that points to elastic or redis as a store; for pinecone-style hosts we map the API. we'll include both examples.
[15:48] Jordan: quick note on function calling — we support function/tool calls and can stream partial outputs; some older transcriptions sometimes mis-label tool names.
[15:56] Maya: streaming latency — will streaming increase token billing substantially if we flush smaller chunks?
[16:02] Priya: token billing is per generated token; streaming chunk size doesn't affect billing but can affect perceived latency. flusher config is tunable.
[16:12] Liam: a security detail — can you rotate keys programmatically? we want automatic rotation after 24 hours for service tokens.
[16:20] Priya: yes you can use token exchange and short-lived tokens; we support automatic rotation via our admin API or vault integration.
[16:28] Diego: do you support mTLS between our proxy and the redwood proxy? some of our compliance requires mTLS.
[16:34] Priya: yes mTLS is supported in Private and Dedicated peering setups; for Hosted we support mutual TLS for certain enterprise setups.
[16:44] [00:16:44] Ana: ok if we map action items — can we get: sdk samples, langchain/llamaindex repo, KMS + SOC2 docs, and a benchmark sheet?
[16:54] Jordan: yes we will deliver those four items.
[16:58] Priya: also the helm chart and proxy config examples.
[17:02] Liam: excellent. last question — what's the onramp time for Dedicated if we decide to buy in september?
[17:10] Jordan: Dedicated onramp is typically 4–8 weeks after signature depending on capacity allocation and network setup. Private is longer. We'll include a proposed timeline in the follow-up.
[17:22] Maya: and what does the pilot contract look like for Hosted credits vs Dedicated trial?
[17:28] Jordan: pilot creds for Hosted are simple self-serve; Dedicated trial typically has a short-term reserved pool for pilot customers with a small monthly commit. we'll outline both.
[17:40] Diego: can we run a small benchmark — 100 concurrent conversations with 3k context — any rough numbers?
[17:48] Priya: we'll run that in our lab and return numbers but rough Hosted numbers for medium models at 100 concurrent is feasible if batching is enabled; exact latency distribution will vary. we'll include a lab run and a test harness.
[17:58] [00:17:58] Jordan: ok wrapping up — recap and next steps. so priya will share sample code, helm chart, langchain + llamaindex examples; i'll send pricing, KMS and SOC2 docs and the Dedicated onboarding timeline; embercloud will produce prompt set and confirm pilot timeline.
[18:18] Ana: yes that matches.
[18:22] Liam: thanks all, this is helpful.
[18:26] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by end of week.
[18:30] (call ends)
